items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Munich Agreement"?
options: The non-aggression pact of 23 August 1939 between Germany and the USSR, with secret terms dividing Poland
A state with dominant global military, economic and political power, such as the USA and USSR after 1945
The principle that members of an organisation act together against an aggressor
The September 1938 agreement by Britain, France, Italy and Germany allowing Germany to take the Sudetenland
items.answer: The September 1938 agreement by Britain, France, Italy and Germany allowing Germany to take the Sudetenland
items.markingKey: D. "Munich Agreement" is the September 1938 agreement by Britain, France, Italy and Germany allowing Germany to take the Sudetenland.

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "The League of Nations achieved nothing." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It settled some disputes in the 1920s, such as the Åland Islands (1921), and its agencies did valuable work on refugees and health.
items.markingKey: It settled some disputes in the 1920s, such as the Åland Islands (1921), and its agencies did valuable work on refugees and health. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between Hitler's actions in 1936–38 and his invasion of Poland in 1939.
items.answer: Earlier actions involved German-speaking areas and were partly tolerated; invading Poland was clear aggression against a non-German state that Britain and France had guaranteed.
items.markingKey: Earlier actions involved German-speaking areas and were partly tolerated; invading Poland was clear aggression against a non-German state that Britain and France had guaranteed. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Justify the relevance of the research question "To what extent was the Munich Agreement of 1938 a reasonable policy for Britain at the time?"
items.answer: It assesses a decision in its context using contemporary evidence.
items.markingKey: It assesses a decision in its context using contemporary evidence. items.stem:
Source A – Historian's interpretation (paraphrased): Paraphrase of A. J. P. Taylor, The Origins of the Second World War, London, 1961

The historian argued that Hitler was not following a fixed blueprint but acted as an opportunist, taking advantage of the weaknesses and mistakes of other powers; he suggested the war of 1939 was more the result of diplomatic blunders than a long-planned war.

What is the message of Source A about the causes of the Second World War: appeasement, expansion and the failure of the League of Nations? Refer to details in the source.
items.answer: The war resulted from opportunism and mistakes rather than a fixed plan.
items.markingKey: The war resulted from opportunism and mistakes rather than a fixed plan. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: Evaluate the research question "What caused WWII?" for an MYP Individuals and Societies investigation into the causes of the Second World War: appeasement, expansion and the failure of the League of Nations. Rewrite it so that it is clear, focused and researchable.
items.answer: Weakness: it is too broad Improved: "To what extent was the Munich Agreement of 1938 a reasonable policy for Britain at the time?"

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The policy, associated with Neville Chamberlain, of making concessions to Hitler to avoid war"?
items.answer: appeasement
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of appeasement.

items.stem: Explain why the Nazi–Soviet Pact made war more likely.
items.answer: It removed the threat of a two-front war for Germany, so Hitler could invade Poland expecting no Soviet resistance.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It removed the threat of a two-front war for Germany, so Hitler could invade Poland expecting no Soviet resistance. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: You have three weeks to investigate "To what extent was the Munich Agreement of 1938 a reasonable policy for Britain at the time?" Outline a step-by-step plan, the sources you would use and one way you would evaluate your process at the end.
items.answer: Use cabinet records, military figures on rearmament, opinion polls and two historians; compare views; evaluate sources; cite in MLA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Use cabinet records, military figures on rearmament, opinion polls and two historians; compare views; evaluate sources; cite in MLA. items.stem:
Source A – Historian's interpretation (paraphrased): Paraphrase of A. J. P. Taylor, The Origins of the Second World War, London, 1961

The historian argued that Hitler was not following a fixed blueprint but acted as an opportunist, taking advantage of the weaknesses and mistakes of other powers; he suggested the war of 1939 was more the result of diplomatic blunders than a long-planned war.

"Appeasement was the main cause of the Second World War." Using Source A and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree?
items.answer: Appeasement contributed by encouraging Hitler, but the primary cause was Nazi expansionism; appeasement explains why he was not stopped earlier rather than why war happened.
items.markingKey: From the source: The war resulted from opportunism and mistakes rather than a fixed plan. Own knowledge for: concessions encouraged Hitler to make further demands; it convinced Hitler that Britain and France would not fight. Own knowledge against: Hitler's ideology and expansionist aims drove the war; the failure of the League and the Nazi–Soviet Pact were also crucial. Judgement: Appeasement contributed by encouraging Hitler, but the primary cause was Nazi expansionism; appeasement explains why he was not stopped earlier rather than why war happened. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. items.stem: Explain why Stalingrad is seen as a turning point in the war.
items.answer: The destruction of the German Sixth Army ended German advances in the east, boosted Soviet morale and began a Red Army advance that continued to Berlin.

items.answer: Most German military losses occurred on the Eastern Front; D-Day opened a second front that hastened defeat.
items.markingKey: Most German military losses occurred on the Eastern Front; D-Day opened a second front that hastened defeat. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "The Battle of Stalingrad was the most important turning point of the Second World War."
items.answer: Thesis: Stalingrad was arguably the decisive turning point in Europe, but the war was global; Midway and US entry were equally important in the Pacific.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it destroyed a German army and began Soviet advances; the Eastern Front was where most German forces were defeated. items.stem: Which battles in 1944 stopped the Japanese invasion of India?
items.answer: Imphal and Kohima
items.markingKey: B. Indian troops formed a large part of the British 14th Army.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the war in Europe and the war in the Pacific.
items.answer: In Europe the decisive fighting was on land, especially on the Eastern Front; in the Pacific, naval and air power and island-hopping were decisive.

items.stem: In 1944, Germany produced about 17,800 tanks and the USSR about 28,963 (approximate figures). Calculate the ratio of Germany's output to the USSR's, and explain how far industrial production explains the outcome of the war.
items.answer: about 0.61 : 1

items.stem: Explain why the outbreak of war in 1939 and the invasion of the USSR in 1941 led to genocide.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The Holocaust was the result of long-term planning by the Nazi leadership."
items.answer: Historians increasingly see a combination: ideology set the goal of removing Jews, while war and competition within the regime radicalised policy into genocide.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: antisemitism was central to Nazi ideology from the start; the Wannsee Conference coordinated genocide across Europe. Arguments against: policy escalated in stages, often radicalised by local officials and war conditions; historians describe a "twisted road" from emigration plans to mass murder. Supported judgement: Historians increasingly see a combination: ideology set the goal of removing Jews, while war and competition within the regime radicalised policy into genocide.

items.stem: Explain why the persecution of Jews in Germany escalated between 1933 and 1939.

items.stem: Explain the difference between genocide and persecution.
items.answer: Persecution is the systematic mistreatment of a group, such as exclusion and violence; genocide is acting with intent to destroy the group.

Plan an extended response to the question: "The United Nations has been more successful than the League of Nations." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: The UN has been more durable and effective in many fields than the League, but its security role remains limited by great-power politics.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: near-universal membership and survival for over 75 years; peacekeeping, humanitarian agencies and human rights law. Thesis/conclusion: The UN has been more durable and effective in many fields than the League, but its security role remains limited by great-power politics. items.stem: Briefly describe the Korean War and the UN and explain what it reveals about the UN in a bipolar world.
items.answer: In 1950 the Security Council authorised military action to defend South Korea while the USSR was boycotting the Council. Collective action was possible only because one superpower was absent.
items.markingKey: Context (In 1950 the Security Council authorised military action to defend South Korea while the USSR was boycotting the Council.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: collective action was possible only because one superpower was absent. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the UN in a bipolar world.

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "The Holocaust was the result of long-term planning by the Nazi leadership." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: Historians increasingly see a combination: ideology set the goal of removing Jews, while war and competition within the regime radicalised policy into genocide.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: antisemitism was central to Nazi ideology from the start; the Wannsee Conference coordinated genocide across Europe. Counter-arguments: policy escalated in stages, often radicalised by local officials and war conditions; historians describe a "twisted road" from emigration plans to mass murder. Thesis/conclusion: Historians increasingly see a combination: ideology set the goal of removing Jews, while war and competition within the regime radicalised policy into genocide. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "Appeasement was the main cause of the Second World War." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: Appeasement contributed by encouraging Hitler, but the primary cause was Nazi expansionism; appeasement explains why he was not stopped earlier rather than why war happened.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: concessions encouraged Hitler to make further demands; it convinced Hitler that Britain and France would not fight. Counter-arguments: Hitler's ideology and expansionist aims drove the war; the failure of the League and the Nazi–Soviet Pact were also crucial. Thesis/conclusion: Appeasement contributed by encouraging Hitler, but the primary cause was Nazi expansionism; appeasement explains why he was not stopped earlier rather than why war happened. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "How significant was the contribution of the Indian Army to Allied victory in Burma between 1943 and 1945?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.
items.answer: Use war diaries, Slim's memoir and two historians; compare troop numbers and campaigns; evaluate sources; cite in MLA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Use war diaries, Slim's memoir and two historians; compare troop numbers and campaigns; evaluate sources; cite in MLA. items.stem:
Source A – Charter (paraphrased): Paraphrase of the Preamble to the Charter of the United Nations, San Francisco, 26 June 1945

The founding document states that the peoples of the United Nations are determined to save future generations from the scourge of war, which twice in their lifetime had brought untold sorrow, and to reaffirm faith in fundamental human rights and the equal rights of nations large and small.

Evaluate Source A as evidence about the consequences of the war: the United Nations and a new world order. Consider its origin, purpose, value and limitations.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of the Preamble to the Charter of the United Nations, San Francisco, 26 June 1945. Purpose: to set out the purposes of the new organisation and win support for it. Value: It shows the aims and values agreed by the founding states. Limitation: It states ideals; it does not show how far states lived up to them, and it was shaped by the victorious powers.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group (UN Genocide Convention, 1948)"?
items.answer: genocide
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of genocide.

items.stem: Which British prime minister signed the Munich Agreement?
items.answer: Neville Chamberlain
items.markingKey: B. He claimed "peace for our time".

items.stem: Which 1943 battle near Kursk was the largest tank battle in history?
items.answer: The Battle of Kursk
items.markingKey: The Battle of Kursk. After it the Red Army held the initiative.

items.stem: Distinguish between the United Nations and the League of Nations.
items.answer: The League lacked the USA and an enforcement mechanism; the UN has near-universal membership and a Security Council able to authorise force, but subject to vetoes.
items.markingKey: The League lacked the USA and an enforcement mechanism; the UN has near-universal membership and a Security Council able to authorise force, but subject to vetoes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Diego writes: "Jews did not resist the Holocaust." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: There was armed resistance, such as the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising (1943), and spiritual and cultural resistance in ghettos and camps.
items.markingKey: There was armed resistance, such as the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising (1943), and spiritual and cultural resistance in ghettos and camps. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Leila writes: "Appeasement was simply cowardice." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Many historians argue it reflected real military, economic and political constraints and bought time for British rearmament.
items.markingKey: Many historians argue it reflected real military, economic and political constraints and bought time for British rearmament. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between the war in the Pacific and the war in Europe.
items.answer: In Europe the decisive fighting was on land, especially on the Eastern Front; in the Pacific, naval and air power and island-hopping were decisive.
items.markingKey: In Europe the decisive fighting was on land, especially on the Eastern Front; in the Pacific, naval and air power and island-hopping were decisive. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "The war ended with a single peace treaty like Versailles." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: There was no single treaty; Germany was occupied and divided, and peace treaties with other countries were signed separately.
items.markingKey: There was no single treaty; Germany was occupied and divided, and peace treaties with other countries were signed separately. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Manchurian Crisis and explain what it reveals about the failure of collective security.
items.answer: After Japan occupied Manchuria in 1931, the League's Lytton Report took a year; Japan left the League in 1933. The League could not act against a great power.
items.markingKey: Context (After Japan occupied Manchuria in 1931, the League's Lytton Report took a year; Japan left the League in 1933.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the League could not act against a great power. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the failure of collective security.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Battle of Stalingrad and explain what it reveals about a turning point on the Eastern Front.
items.answer: From August 1942 to February 1943 Soviet forces defended the city and encircled the German Sixth Army in Operation Uranus. It marked the start of German retreat in the east.
items.markingKey: Context (From August 1942 to February 1943 Soviet forces defended the city and encircled the German Sixth Army in Operation Uranus.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: it marked the start of German retreat in the east. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to a turning point on the Eastern Front.

items.stem: Data from United Nations: UN member states – 1945: 51 members; 1965: 117 members. By what percentage did it change over the period? Show your working.
items.markingKey: Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100 (M1) = (117 − 51) ÷ 51 × 100 = +129.4% (A1). Dividing by the new value is a common error.

items.stem:
Source A – Diary (summarised): Summary of Anne Frank, diary written 1942–44, first published as Het Achterhuis, Amsterdam, 1947

A Jewish teenager hiding with her family in a secret annex in Amsterdam recorded daily life, fears of discovery and hopes for the future between 1942 and 1944. The family was discovered and deported in August 1944; she died in Bergen-Belsen in 1945.

Explain one value and one limitation of Source A for an investigation into the Holocaust: persecution, genocide and responses, referring to its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Summary of Anne Frank, diary written 1942–44, first published as Het Achterhuis, Amsterdam, 1947. Purpose: originally a private diary, later revised by the author with a view to publication after the war. Value: It gives a personal, contemporary view of persecution and life in hiding. Limitation: It reflects one family's experience in hiding and does not describe the camps or the experience of the majority of victims.

items.stem:
Source A – Historian's interpretation (paraphrased): Paraphrase of A. J. P. Taylor, The Origins of the Second World War, London, 1961

The historian argued that Hitler was not following a fixed blueprint but acted as an opportunist, taking advantage of the weaknesses and mistakes of other powers; he suggested the war of 1939 was more the result of diplomatic blunders than a long-planned war.

How reliable is Source A for someone researching the causes of the Second World War: appeasement, expansion and the failure of the League of Nations? Justify your answer using its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of A. J. P. Taylor, The Origins of the Second World War, London, 1961. Purpose: to challenge the view that Hitler alone planned the war. Value: It provoked important debate and considered the role of other powers. Limitation: Many historians argue it underplays Hitler's ideology and aims set out in Mein Kampf.

items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why Midway was a turning point in the Pacific.
items.answer: Japan lost four carriers and experienced aircrews it could not replace, so the US gained the initiative and moved to the offensive.

items.stem: "The Battle of Stalingrad was the most important turning point of the Second World War." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Stalingrad was arguably the decisive turning point in Europe, but the war was global; Midway and US entry were equally important in the Pacific.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it destroyed a German army and began Soviet advances; the Eastern Front was where most German forces were defeated.
